newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu's Zaire clan faces uncertain future.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu's Zaire clan faces uncertain future.

text.p: Faced with the end of decades of privilege and possible revenge from an angry populace, the clan surrounding Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko faces an uncertain future.
So do numerous other hangers-on who hitched their fortune to the Mobutu regime over the last 32 years.

While his closest family accompanied Mobutu to Congo for talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila, some of his Ngbandi tribe who profited from his rule and other associates are left to fend themselves as the rebels close in on Kinshasa.
Some have already switched sides. Others have left Zaire or sent their families abroad.
"The armed opposition has taken up weapons to finish with this system that became self-perpetuating," one legislator from Mobutu's home region said last month explaining his conversion.
"The president has been constantly ill and absent."
A final communique issued after talks between Mobutu and Kabila on board a South African ship said Mobutu had offered to hand over power to an elected successor.
But the rebel side said this was not acceptable, that power should be transferred to Kabila and that its troops would fight on while Mobutu considered the demand to quit.

Rebels already hold Mobutu's northern riverside birthplace at Lisala and are heading for the palace in the jungle he built at vast expense at his ancestral homeland of Gbadolite among the Ngbandi, a tiny minority within Zaire's over 200 tribes.
Mobutu's wife Bobi Ladawa and his son Nzanga travelled with him to Congo as part of a delegation of at least 50 people.
Also with the team is chief negotiator and nephew, Honore Ngbanda, nicknamed "The Terminator" as former head of Zaire's repressive security apparatus in the early 1990s.
But left behind in Kinshasa are any number of generals and soldiers who have retreated before the relentless rebel advance.
Residents say they are worried the frightened troops may make a last stand in Kinshasa and that their last orders will be for the destruction of what remains.
Among those left behind is General Nzimbe Nzale, commander of the Special Presidential Division, the only elite unit in Zaire which draws heavily on the Ngbandi and related tribes.
"We must fight to the death to defend Kinshasa," Nzimbe said, berating his soldiers in a recent television broadcast.
But Kinshasa's military governor on Saturday told soliders to stay calm and protect everyone regardless of their origins.
"They must defend and protect everyone in the same way, without taking account of race, ethnic or regional origins," General Amela Lokima told state radio.
Not only the Ngbandi gained from Mobutu's rule.
Political cunning assured an opulent lifestyle for anyone who would accept the system of institutionalised corruption and not threaten the president -- even former enemies.
Many of the elite have switched off mobile telephones that were essential accesories of their lifestyle as they flee the country or try to keep a low profile.
